translations.text: The Book of the Laws of Countries.
Some days ago we went up to visit our brother Shemashgram, and Bardaisan came and found us there.
After feeling him and seeing that he was well, he asked us, “What were you talking about? I heard your voices from outside as I was coming in.”
For whenever he found us discussing something before he arrived, he used to ask us, “What were you saying?”
so that he could discuss it with us. We said to him, “Avida was saying this to us:
‘If there is one God, as you say, and he made human beings and desires them to do what you command,
why did he not make human beings so that they could not sin, but would always do what is good?
For in this way his will would be fulfilled.’” Bardaisan said to him, “Tell me, my son Avida, what do you have in mind?
That there is not one God of all, or that there is one, but he does not want human beings to conduct themselves justly and rightly?”
Avida said, “My lord, I asked these men of my own age to give me an answer.” Bardaisan said to him:
“If you want to learn, it will help you to learn from someone older than they are. But if you want to teach, there is no need for you to question them.
Instead, you should allow them to ask you whatever they wish. For teachers are questioned;
they do not ask questions. And when they do ask questions, it is to correct the questioner’s thinking so that he may ask properly, and to discover what he wants.
For it is a good thing to know how to ask questions.” Avida said, “I do want to learn.
But I began by questioning these brothers of mine because I feel shy before you.” Bardaisan said, “You speak modestly.
But know that anyone who asks properly, wants to be convinced, and approaches the path of truth without quarrelling has no reason to feel ashamed.
For by these things I have mentioned he gives pleasure to the person being questioned. So, my son, if you have some thought about the matter you asked about, tell it to all of us.
If it seems right to us too, we will agree with you. But if it does not seem right to us, we are obliged to show you why it does not.
But if you only want to understand this matter, without having any opinion about it yourself,
like someone who has only recently joined the disciples and is asking questions for the first time, I will explain it to you so that you do not leave us empty-handed.
And if what I tell you pleases you, you have this and other things as well to learn from us.
But if it does not please you, we, for our part, speak without grudging.” Avida said, “I too am very willing to listen
and be convinced. For I did not hear this idea from anyone else.
Rather, I expressed it to these brothers of mine from my own thinking, and they were unwilling to convince me. Instead, they say, ‘Simply believe,
and you will be able to understand everything.’ But I cannot believe unless I am convinced.” Bardaisan said:
It is not Avida alone who is unwilling to believe, but many others too. Because they have no faith, they cannot be persuaded either.
Instead, they are always tearing down and building up, and they prove to be empty of all knowledge of the truth.
But since Avida is unwilling to believe, I will speak to you who believe about this matter he has asked about, so that he too may hear something more.
And he began to say to us: “There are many people who have no faith and have received no knowledge from the wisdom of truth.
For this reason they are unable to speak and reach a conclusion, nor do they readily venture to listen.
For they have no foundation of faith on which to build, and no confidence on which to rest their hope.
And because they are full of doubts even about God, they do not have the fear of him within them, which would free them from all other fears.
For anyone who does not have the fear of God within him is enslaved to every fear.
They are not even certain that they are right to disbelieve what they disbelieve. Instead, their thoughts wander, and they cannot stand firm.
The taste of their thoughts is insipid in their mouths, and they are always anxious and alarmed
and presumptuous. Now, as for Avida’s question, ‘Why did God not make us so that we would not sin and be condemned?’
If a human being had been made that way, he would not have existed in his own right, but would have been an instrument of whoever moved him.
And it is obvious that whoever moved him would move him as he wished, either toward good or toward evil.
How, then, would a human being differ from a harp that someone else plays, or from a chariot that someone else drives?
Praise and blame depend on the skill of the one using them. The harp itself does not know what is being played on it, nor does the chariot know whether it is being pulled and driven well.
Rather, they are instruments made for the use of someone who has knowledge. But God, in his kindness, did not wish to make the human being that way.
Instead, through freedom he exalted him above many things and made him equal to the angels. For look at the sun, the moon, and the constellations,
and at the rest of the things that are greater than we are in some respect: they have not been given freedom of their own.
Instead, they are all bound by a command to do only what they have been commanded, and nothing else.
For the sun has never said, ‘I will not rise at my appointed time,’ nor has the moon said, ‘I will not change, nor wane, nor wax.’
Not one of the stars has said, ‘I will not rise or set,’ nor has the sea said, ‘I will not carry ships or remain within my boundaries.’
Nor have the mountains said, ‘We will not remain in the places where we were set,’ nor have the winds said, ‘We will not blow.’
Nor has the earth said, ‘I will not carry and support everything above me.’ Instead, all things serve and are subject to a single command.
For they are instruments of God’s unerring wisdom. If everything were serving, who would be served?
And if everything were being served, who would be serving? Then nothing would be different from anything else.
For whatever is one and has no division within it is an entity that has not yet been fashioned.
But those things needed for service were placed under human control, because the human being was made in the image of God.
For this reason, these things were kindly given to him to serve him for a time. He was also allowed to govern himself according to his own will.
Whatever he is able to do, he may do if he wishes; and if he does not wish, he need not do it. He himself may earn merit or incur blame.
For if he had been made unable to do evil, so that he could not incur guilt through it, then neither would the good he did have been his own.
Nor could he have earned merit through it. For when someone does good or evil without acting of his own will, his merit and his blame
lie in the hands of the one who compels him. From this, you can see that God's grace toward humanity is great,
and that humanity has been given greater freedom than all these elements we have spoken about.
Through this freedom, a person may earn merit, conduct himself in a godly way, and mingle with the angels, who themselves also possess freedom of their own
selves. For we understand that if the angels themselves had not possessed freedom of their own,
they would not have joined themselves to human women, nor sinned, nor fallen from their places.
Likewise, the others who did their Lord's will were exalted and made holy through their own free choice, and received great gifts.
For everyone who exists depends on the Lord of all, and his gifts have no limit.
Nevertheless, understand that even those things I said were established by commands are not entirely deprived of all freedom.
For this reason, on the last day they are all subject to judgment. I said to him, “How, then, are things that are fixed subject to judgment?”
He said to me, “Philip, the elements are not judged in the respect in which they are fixed, but in the respect in which they have control.
For entities are not deprived of their nature when they are fashioned, but the intensity of their original purity is diminished through their mixture with one another.
They are subjected by the power of their Maker. They are not judged in the respect in which they are subjected, but for what belongs to them.” Avida said to him,
“What you have said is very good. But the commandments given to human beings are difficult, and they cannot carry them out.”
Bardaisan said, “This is the statement of someone who does not wish to do good, and especially of someone who has obediently submitted to his enemy.
For human beings have only been commanded to do what they are able to do. For there are two
commandments set before us, which are fitting and appropriate to freedom itself: one is that we keep away from everything evil that we would hate to have happen to us;
and the other is that we do what is good, which we love and wish would happen to us as well. Who, then, is too weak to refrain from stealing,
or from lying, or from committing adultery and sexual immorality, or from hating and deceiving?
For all these things are under the control of a person's mind. They do not happen through bodily strength, but through the will of the soul.
For even if someone is poor, sick, old, and disabled in his limbs, he can refrain from doing all these things.
And just as he can refrain from doing these things, so he can love, bless, speak the truth, and pray for the well-being of everyone he knows.
And if he is healthy and has the means, he can also give something from what he has. He can also use his bodily strength to support someone who is sick and broken.
Who, then, is this person who cannot do so, about whom those lacking faith complain? I do not know. For I think
that a person is more capable of carrying out these commandments than of anything else. For they are easy, and nothing can hinder them.
For we have not been commanded to carry heavy loads of stones, wood, or anything else—things that only the physically strong can do.
Nor have we been commanded to build fortresses and establish cities, something that only kings can do.
Nor to steer a ship, which only sailors know how to steer. Nor to measure out land and divide it, something that only surveyors
know how to do. Nor have we been commanded to practice any of the crafts that some people possess while the rest lack them.
Rather, in God's kindness, commandments have been given to us without stint, which every person who has a soul can carry out with joy.
For there is no one who does not rejoice when he does what is good, nor anyone who avoids evil deeds who does not feel pleasure in his soul,
except those who were not created for this good and are called weeds.
For the Judge is not unjust, so as to condemn someone for something he cannot do. Avida said to him:
“So, Bardaisan, are you saying that these deeds are easy to do?” Bardaisan said: “I said, and I say, that they are easy for someone who is willing.
For this is the good conduct of a free mind and of a soul that has not rebelled against its guides.
For many things hinder bodily activity, especially old age, sickness, and poverty.”
Avida said: “Perhaps a person can avoid evil deeds. But who among human beings can do good deeds?”
Bardaisan said: “It is easier to do good than to avoid evil. For goodness belongs to human nature.
That is why a person rejoices when he does good. Evil, however, is the work of the Enemy.
That is why a person does evil deeds when he is disturbed and his nature is not healthy. For know, my son, that for someone to praise and bless his friend is an easy
thing. But for someone not to provoke and insult a person he hates is not easy. Nevertheless, it can be done.
And when someone does what is good, his mind is at ease and his conscience is clear, and he is willing for everyone to see what he has done.
But when someone sins and does harm, he is troubled and disturbed, full of fury and anger, and tormented in soul and body.
And while he is in this state of mind, he is not willing to be seen by everyone. And those things in which he rejoices, which are followed by praise and blessing,
are withheld from him. But those things that trouble and disturb him are followed by condemnation from everyone. But perhaps someone will say:
For even fools find relief when they do filthy things, but not when these things are done to them, nor when they are praised.
Nor is it based on a good hope, nor does that pleasure remain with them. For the relief that comes in health, based on a good hope, is one thing,
and the relief of sickness, which comes with a bad expectation, is another. For desire is one thing, and love another,
and affection another, and companionship another. We should readily understand that counterfeit affection is called desire.
Although it offers relief for a moment, it is very far from true affection, whose relief is never spoiled
or undone. I said to him, “This Avida also used to say the same thing: that a person sins by his very nature.
For if he were not capable of sinning, he would not sin.” Bardaisan said, “If all people performed the same deed
and followed the same way of thinking, it would be clear that their nature was directing them,
and that they did not have the freedom I told you about. But so that you may understand what nature is and what freedom is,
I will tell you more. Human nature is this: to be born, to grow, to reach maturity, to have children, and to grow old, while eating and drinking,
sleeping and waking, and to die. Because these things belong to nature, they are found among all people,
and not only among all people, but also among all animals that have life in them.
Some of them are found among trees as well. For this is the work of nature, which makes, creates, and establishes everything as it has been commanded.
Nature is also found to be preserved among animals in their actions. For a lion eats meat by its nature,
and therefore all lions are meat-eaters. A sheep eats grass, and therefore all sheep are grass-eaters.
A bee makes honey, on which it feeds. Therefore all bees are honey-makers.
An ant stores provisions for itself in summer, on which to feed in winter. Therefore all ants do this.
A scorpion strikes with its sting someone who has not harmed it, and all scorpions strike in this way.
All animals preserve their nature: meat-eaters do not eat fodder, and fodder-eaters do not eat meat.
Human beings, however, do not conduct themselves in this way. In matters concerning their bodies, they preserve nature like the animals. But in matters
concerning their minds, they do whatever they wish, as free beings with authority over themselves, and as the likeness of God. For some of them eat meat
and do not touch bread. Some distinguish between meat dishes, while others eat no flesh at all from any animal that has life in it.
Some have sexual relations with their mothers, their sisters, and their daughters, while others do not approach even their own wives.
Some avenge themselves like lions and leopards, while others, like scorpions, harm those who have done them no wrong.
Others are led like sheep and do not harm those who lead them. Some conduct themselves with kindness, and others with justice.
And there are some who live wickedly. If anyone says of each of them, “It is his nature to act this way,” let him see that this is not how matters stand.
For there are some who were sexually immoral and drunkards, but when the discipline of good advice reached them, they became chaste and self-controlled.
They despised the desires of their bodies. And there are some who conducted themselves chastely and with self-control,
but when they neglected sound discipline and treated the commandments of God and of their teachers with contempt, they fell away from the path of truth.
They became sexually immoral and dissolute. And there are some who repented again after their fall: fear came upon them, and they returned to the truth in which they had stood.
What, then, is human nature, seeing that all human beings differ from one another in their conduct and their choices?
Those who have held to the same way of thinking and the same counsel resemble one another. But those people who, up to
now, are enticed by their desires and driven by their anger want to lay the wrong they do upon their Maker,
so that they themselves may be found innocent of wrongdoing, while the one who made them is condemned by an empty accusation.
They do not consider that nature is not subject to law. For no one is blamed for being tall,
or short, or white, or black, or for having large or small eyes, or for any bodily defect.
But a person is blamed if he steals or lies, commits fraud, poisons or insults others, or does things like these.
From this the matter becomes clear: for things that are not within our power but come to us by nature, we are not condemned,
nor are we acquitted on their account. But as for the things we do by our own free will, if they are good,
we are acquitted and praised for them; and if they are evil, we are condemned and blamed for them. Again we questioned him and said to him,
“There are others who say that human beings are governed by the decree of Fate, sometimes acting badly and sometimes well.”
He said to us, “I too, Philip and Bar-Yamma, know that there are people called Chaldeans,
and others who love this knowledge of their art, just as I too once loved it.
For I have said elsewhere that the human soul longs to know something that many others do not know.
These men hold that what people do—all the wrong they do and all the good they do,
and everything that happens to them, in wealth and poverty, in sickness and health, and in bodily impairments—
comes upon them through the governance of those stars called the Seven, and is governed by them. But there are others who say the opposite:
that this art of the Chaldeans is false, or that Fate itself does not exist but is an empty name.
All matters, great and small, lie within human power, while bodily impairments and defects occur by chance
and happen to a person. Still others say that everything a person does, he does by his own choice, through the freedom given to him.
And the defects, failings, and unpleasant things that happen to him he receives from God as punishment.
But to me, limited as my understanding is, it seems that all three of these schools of thought speak the truth in some respects and speak falsely in others.
They speak the truth because they speak on the basis of the appearances that human beings observe, and because they too,
being human, see how circumstances press upon them. But they speak falsely because God's wisdom surpasses them:
the wisdom that established the worlds, created humanity, appointed rulers, and gave everything the authority appropriate to each.
Now I say that this authority belongs to God, to the angels, to the powers, to the rulers, and to the elements,
and to human beings and animals. All these orders that I have mentioned have not been given authority over everything.
For only one has authority over everything. Rather, they have authority in some matters and no authority in others,
as I said before, so that God's goodness may be seen in what they have authority over, and so that, through what they have no authority over, they may know
that they have a Lord. There is, then, fate, as the Chaldeans say. That not everything happens according to our will is evident from this:
most people would like to be rich, to have authority over their companions, to be healthy in body, and to have circumstances obey them as they wish.
Yet wealth is found only among a few, authority only among isolated individuals, and bodily health is not found among all people.
Those who are rich do not fully enjoy their wealth, nor do circumstances obey those in authority as they wish.
Sometimes circumstances fail to obey them, contrary to their wishes. Sometimes the rich grow richer, as they desire,
and sometimes they become poor, contrary to their desires. Those who are utterly poor live in conditions they do not want,
and pass their lives in the world in ways they do not desire. They long for things, but those things elude them. Many have children but do not raise them.
Others raise them but do not enjoy them. Others enjoy them, but they become a source of disgrace and pain. Others grow rich, as they wish,
but become sick, contrary to their wishes. Others become healthy, as they wish, but become poor, contrary to their wishes.
Some have many of the things they want and few of the things they do not want. Others have many of the things they do not want
and few of the things they want. Thus it is found that possessions, honors, health,
illnesses, children, and the various things people desire are subject to fate and are not under our authority. But when things happen as we wish,
we are pleased with them and rejoice; and we are forcibly dragged toward things we do not want.
From the things that happen to us against our wishes, it is evident that even the things we desire
do not happen to us because we want them. Rather, they happen as they happen,
and we are pleased with some of them and not with others. And we human beings are found to be governed equally by nature.
and especially by fate, and by our free will, each person as he wishes. But now let us speak and show that fate does not have power over everything.
For the very thing called fate is an ordered course of movement given by God to the ruling powers and the elements.
According to this movement and order, the [?] undergo changes through their effects upon the soul, and souls undergo changes through their effects upon bodies.
This process of change is called fate and the horoscope of birth of this assemblage, which is mixed and purified to help that which, through God's mercy and grace,
has been helped and continues to be helped until the completion of everything. The body, then, is governed by nature, while the soul also suffers and feels along with it.
The body is neither constrained nor helped by fate in all the things it does, one by one.
For a man does not become a father before fifteen years of age, nor does a woman become a mother before thirteen years of age.
Likewise, old age also has a law: women cease bearing children, and men are cut off
from the natural capacity to reproduce. Other animals, which are also governed by their own nature, before the ages I have mentioned,
not only reproduce but also grow too old to reproduce, just as human bodies also cease to reproduce when they grow old.
Fate cannot give them children at a time when the body does not have the natural capacity to produce them.
Nor, again, can fate keep a human body alive without food and drink.
Nor, even when it has food and drink, can fate grant that it will not die. For these things, and many others, belong to nature.
But when nature's times and ways have run their course, then fate comes and becomes apparent among these things.
It produces things that differ from one another. Sometimes it helps nature and makes it flourish, and sometimes it harms and disfigures it.
The body's growth and maturity come from nature. But diseases and defects in the body occur outside nature and through fate.
The union of males and females, and the pleasure of both parties, come from nature. But hatred comes from fate,
as do the dissolution of the union and all the impurity and indecency that people commit in their lust under the pretext of union.
Childbirth and children come from nature. But through fate children are sometimes deformed, sometimes miscarried, and sometimes die before their time.
From nature comes satisfaction in due measure for all bodies. But from fate come a lack of food and bodily distress.
Likewise, from fate also come gluttony and unnecessary extravagance. Nature commands
that elders should be judges over the young, and the wise over fools, and that the strong should be leaders over the weak, and the courageous over the timid.
But fate makes children leaders over elders, and fools over the wise, and in time of war makes the weak command the strong,
and the timid command the courageous. Understand this simply: whenever nature is thrown into disorder and departs from its proper course, fate is the cause of its disorder.
For the chiefs and governors through whom the process of change called the horoscope of birth takes place are opposed to one another.
Among them, those that help nature and add to its beauty when their course favors them are called those of the right.
They stand in the exalted places of the zodiac, in their own allotted portions. Those of the left are called evil.
When they too occupy exalted places, they oppose nature. They harm not only human beings,
but sometimes also animals, trees, fruits, the seasons of the year, springs of water, and everything in nature that is under their rule.
Because of these divisions and conflicts among the ruling powers, some people have supposed that the world is governed without providence,
because they did not know that these conflicts and divisions, victories and defeats, arise from actions that God has granted freedom to perform.
For they too are agents with authority over themselves, either to conquer or to be defeated. Just as we see fate overpowering nature,
so we can also see human freedom pushing fate aside and overpowering it, though not in everything, just as
fate itself does not push nature aside in everything. For it is fitting that all three—the affairs of nature, of fate, and of freedom—
should be preserved in their activity until the course is completed and the measure and number are fulfilled, as seemed right to the one who commanded
how the existence and final end of all creatures, and the continued existence of all beings and natures, should be. Avida said:
“From what you have shown, I am convinced that a human being does not sin because of his nature, and that not all people conduct themselves alike.
But if you can also show this—that those who sin do not sin because of fate and its decree—
then it will be right to believe that a human being possesses his own freedom, and by his nature approaches good things and guards against evil things,
and that for this reason he is also justly judged on the last day.” Bardaisan said: “From the fact that people do not all conduct themselves alike, you have become convinced
that they do not sin because of their nature. The matter therefore requires you to be convinced that neither do they sin entirely because of their fate,
if we can show you that the decree of the fates and ruling powers does not move all people alike, but that we have freedom within ourselves,
so that we need not serve physical nature or be moved by the governance of the ruling powers.” Avida said: “Show me this, and I will be convinced by you,
and I will do whatever you command me.” Bardaisan said: “Have you read the books of the Chaldeans in Babylon,
in which it is written what the stars do through their combinations at people's births,
and the books of the Egyptians, in which all the kinds of things that happen to people are written?” Avida said:
“I have read books of Chaldean astrology, but I do not know which are Babylonian and which are Egyptian.” Bardaisan said:
“The teaching of both countries is the same.” Avida said: “It is clear that this is so.” Bardaisan said:
“Listen now and understand: not all people throughout the earth alike carry out what the stars decree through their allotted places and portions.
For people have established laws in each country through the freedom given to them by God. For the gift
This runs counter to the portion allotted to the rulers: they take for themselves something that has not been given to them. I will begin to speak.
As far as I remember, I will begin with the East, the starting point of the whole world. The laws of the Seres. The Seres have laws
that they must not kill, commit sexual immorality, or worship idols. Throughout the land of the Seres there are no idols, nor any prostitute
who kills a man, nor anyone who is killed, although they too are born at every hour and on every day.
Fierce Mars, when positioned in the middle of the heavens, does not compel the free will of the Seres to make a man shed his fellow's blood with an iron weapon.
Nor does Venus, when positioned with Mars, compel any man among the Seres to have sexual relations with his fellow's wife
or with another woman. Yet there are rich and poor people there, sick and healthy people, rulers and subjects,
because these things have been placed under the authority of the celestial governors. The law of the Brahmins in India. Again, among the Indians there is a law for the Brahmins,
of whom there are many thousands and tens of thousands, that they must not commit murder, worship idols, or commit sexual immorality,
eat meat, or drink wine. Among these people, not one of these things occurs.
These people have now lived for thousands of years according to this law that they established for themselves. Another law in India.
There is another law in India, in the same region, for those who are neither of Brahmin ancestry nor followers of their teaching:
they worship idols, commit sexual immorality, kill, and do other hateful things that the Brahmins do not approve of.
In that same region of India there are people who customarily eat human flesh, just as the rest of the nations eat the flesh of animals.
The evil stars have not compelled the Brahmins to do evil and impure things,
nor have the good stars persuaded the rest of the Indians not to do evil.
Nor have those stars that are favorably positioned in their proper places and in the human signs of the zodiac persuaded those who eat human flesh
not to consume impure and hateful foods. The law of the Persians. Again, they established laws for themselves—
the Persians—that they should take their sisters, their daughters, and their daughters' daughters as wives.
Some go further and even marry their mothers. Some of these Persians dispersed and settled in Media, in the land of the Parthians, in Parthia,
in Egypt, and in Phrygia. They are called Magi. In every country and region where they have settled, they live according to this law established for their ancestors.
We cannot say that for all the Magi and the rest of the Persians, Venus is positioned with the moon and with Saturn in Saturn's house, in her allotted degrees,
with Mars bearing witness to them. There are many places in the kingdom of the Parthians where men kill their wives, their brothers, and their sons
without incurring blame. But among the Romans and Greeks, anyone who kills one of these
incurs a severe punishment for the offense. The laws of the Gauls. Among the Gauls, it is the women who sow and reap, build and work.
All the tasks of laborers. They do not wear colored clothes, put on shoes, or use fine ointments.
No one reproaches them when they commit adultery with strangers or have intercourse with the slaves of their households.
Their husbands, the men of Gaul, wear colored clothes, adorn themselves with gold and beads, and anoint themselves with fine ointments.
They do not behave this way because of weakness, but because of the law established for them. They are all men who love hunting and engage in fighting.
We cannot say that for all the women of Gaul, Venus is positioned in Capricorn or Aquarius, in a place of misfortune.
Nor is it possible to say of all the men of Gaul that Mars and Venus are positioned in Aries, where it is written that vigorous and pampered men are born. Laws
of the Bactrians. Among the Bactrians, who are called Kushans, women adorn themselves with fine men's clothing,
with much gold and fine beads. Male and female slaves serve them more than their husbands.
They ride horses, adorned with gold ornaments and precious stones. These women do not preserve their chastity,
but have intercourse with their slaves and with strangers who come to that country. Their husbands do not reproach them,
and they have no fear, because the Kushans regard their wives as mistresses.
We cannot say that for all Bactrian women, Venus and Mars are positioned
with Mercury in the house of Mars at midheaven, where wealthy, adulterous women are born who subject their husbands to themselves in everything.
Laws of the people of Petra, Edessa, and Arabia. Among the people of Petra, Edessa, and Arabia,
not only is a woman who commits adultery put to death, but even a woman who has a reputation for adultery receives punishment.
Laws in Hatra. A law is established in Hatra that anyone who steals a small object, even if it is worth [?], is to be stoned. Among the Kushans,
they spit in the face of someone who commits such a theft. Among the Romans, someone who commits a petty theft is flogged and released.
Beyond the Euphrates and eastward, someone who is insulted as a thief or a murderer does not become very angry.
But if someone is insulted as a man who sleeps with males, he seeks the other's life, even to the point of killing him. Laws [?]
Among [?], boys [?] and are not condemned. Again, throughout the whole country of the East, those who are insulted in this way and become known for it—
their fathers and brothers kill them. Often they do not even make their graves known. Laws of the people of the East.
In the north, however, in the country of the Germans and their neighbors, the handsome young men among them become like wives to men.
They even hold wedding feasts for them. They do not regard this as a disgrace or an insult, because of their established law.
It is not possible that for all those in Gaul who suffer this disgrace, Mercury should be positioned in their birth charts
with Venus in the house of Saturn, within the bounds of Mars and in the western signs of the zodiac. For it is concerning men born in this way that it is written:
who are dishonored like women. Laws of the Britons. Among the Britons, many men marry one woman.
Laws of the Parthians. Among the Parthians, one man marries many women, and all of them obey his commands chastely,
because of the law established there in that country. Laws of the Amazons. The Amazons, an entire nation, have no husbands.
Instead, like animals, once a year, in spring, they leave their territory and cross the river. When they have crossed,
they hold a great festival on the mountain, and men come from those territories and stay with them for fourteen days.
They have intercourse with them, and the women become pregnant by them. Then the women cross back
to their own country. When they give birth, they throw away the male children and raise the females. It is well known that, as nature directs,
because they all conceive in the same month, they also give birth in the same month, a little earlier or a little later. And as we have heard,
they are all vigorous and warlike. Not one of the stars can help all those male children who are born, so that they will not be thrown away.
The Book of the Chaldeans. It is written in the Book of the Chaldeans that when Mercury is positioned with Venus in the house of Mercury,
it produces painters, sculptors, and bankers. But when they are in the house of Venus,
they produce perfumers, dancers, singers, and poets. Yet throughout the whole country of the Arabs and the Saracens, in Upper Libya,
among the Mauritanians, in the country of Numrus [?] at the mouth of the Ocean, in Outer Germany, and in Upper Sarmatia,
in Spain, in all the countries north of Pontus, throughout the country of the Alans, among the Albanians, and among the Tsatsians [?],
and in Brusa [?], beyond the Duru [?], no one sees sculptors, painters, perfumers, bankers, or poets.
But is the decree of Mercury and Venus absent from the entire circuit of the world? Throughout Media, all people, when they are dying,
while life is still in them, fall prey to dogs, and dogs eat the dead of all Media.
We cannot say that all Medes are born with the moon positioned with Mars in Cancer, by day, below the earth.
For it is written that those whom dogs eat are born in this way. All Indians, when they die, are
burned in fire, and many of their wives are burned alive with them. We cannot say that all the Indian women who are burned
have Mars and the sun positioned in their horoscopes in Leo, by night, below the earth, as is the case at the birth of people who are burned in fire.
All Germans die by strangulation, except those who are killed in battle.
It is impossible for all Germans to have the moon and the ascendant positioned between Mars and Saturn in their horoscopes.
Rather, in every country, every day and at every hour, people are born with horoscopes that differ from one another.
Human laws prevail over the decree, and people conduct themselves according to their customs. Fate does not compel the Seres to commit murder when they do not wish to.
Nor the Brahmans to eat meat, nor the Persians to refrain from marrying their daughters and sisters, nor the Indians to refrain from burning.
Nor the Medes to keep dogs from eating them, nor the Parthians to refrain from marrying many wives.
Nor the Britons to refrain from having many men marry one woman, nor the Edessenes to abandon chastity.
Nor the Greeks to refrain from holding athletic contests, … nor the Romans to refrain from continually conquering territories, nor the Geli to refrain from marrying one another.
Nor the Amazons to raise males. Nor has the birth horoscope compelled people throughout the world to practice the art of the Muses.
But, as I said, in every place and among every people, all human beings use the freedom of their nature as they wish. And they serve fate and nature because of
the body they wear—sometimes as they wish and sometimes against their wishes. For in every place and among every people there are rich and poor,
rulers and subjects, healthy and sick, each according to what fate and the birth horoscope have allotted him. I said to him:
“You have convinced us of these things, our father Bardaisan, and we know that they are true. But you know that the Chaldeans say
that the earth is divided into seven portions called zones, and that each of these seven rules over one of the portions.
In each of these regions, the will of its ruler prevails, and this is called law.”
He said to me, “First, know, my son Philip, that the Chaldeans devised this argument as an excuse for their error.
For even if the earth is divided into seven portions, nevertheless in each one of these portions
many laws are found that differ from one another. For there are not seven laws in the world corresponding to the number of the seven planets,
nor twelve corresponding to the number of the signs of the zodiac, nor thirty-six corresponding to the number of the decans.
Rather, there are many laws in every kingdom, every country, every district, and every settlement, differing from those of their neighbors.
For you remember that I told you that in the same zone of the Indians there are people who do not eat animal flesh,
and there are others who eat human flesh. I also told you about the Persians and the Magi,
that they married their daughters and sisters not only in the zone of Persia, but in every place they traveled
to, they followed the law of their ancestors and preserved the mysteries of what had been handed down to them.
Remember also that I told you of many peoples scattered throughout the whole world, who are not in one zone
but in every direction and in every zone, and who do not possess the craft that Hermes and Beltis bestow when they are in conjunction with one another.
If the laws belonged to the zones, this could not happen. But the reason is clear:
these people, in their way of life, keep far from mingling with the mass of humanity.
How many wise men do you think have abolished laws in their own countries that seemed to them to have been poorly established?
And how many laws have been repealed because of necessity! And how many kings, when they took possession of lands that were not their own,
abolished their established laws and enacted whatever laws they wanted! And when these things happen,
not one of the stars can preserve the law. Here is a recent example for you to consider: just yesterday the Romans took possession of Arabia,
and abolished all the laws that had existed before their arrival, especially the circumcision that people used to practice.
For a person who has authority over himself obeys the law imposed on him by another who likewise possesses authority over himself.
But I will tell you something that can persuade the foolish and those lacking faith more than anything else: all the Jews who received the law through Moses
circumcise their male children on the eighth day. They do not wait for the arrival of the stars, nor do they renounce the law
of their country. Nor does the star ruling the region compel them. Rather, whether they are in Edom or Arabia or Greece or Persia, whether in the north or in the south,
they observe this law laid down for them by their ancestors. And it is clear that what they do does not come from their horoscope.
For it is impossible for Ares to be in position for all Jews on the eighth day, when they are circumcised,
so that iron should pass over them and their blood be shed. And wherever they are, none of them worship idols.
Once every seven days they and their children cease from all work, all building, all travel,
and buying and selling. They do not slaughter animals on the Sabbath, light fires, or judge cases.
And no one is found among them whom fate commands on the Sabbath to go to court and win, or go to court and lose, or demolish or build,
or do any of the things done by all those people who have not accepted this law. They also have other practices
in which they do not conduct themselves like the rest of humanity, although on this very day they both give birth and are born, fall ill and die.
For these things are not under human control. In Syria and Edessa, men used to cut off their genitals in honor of Atargatis.
But when King Abgar came to believe, he ordered that anyone who cut off his genitals should have his hand cut off. And from that day until now,
no one has cut off his genitals in the territory of Edessa. And what shall we say about our new people, the Christians, whom in every country and every region
Christ established at his coming? For wherever we are, we are all called Christians after the one name of Christ, and we gather on the same day, Sunday.
On the appointed days we abstain from food. Our brothers in Gaul do not marry males, nor do those in Parthia marry two wives.
Those in Judea are not circumcised, nor do our sisters among the Gelae and the Kushans have intercourse with strangers.
Those in Persia do not marry their daughters, nor do those in Media flee from their dead, or bury them while they are alive,
or give them to dogs as food. Nor do those in Edessa kill their wives who commit adultery, or their sisters.
Instead, they separate themselves from them and leave them to God's judgment. Nor do those in Hatra stone thieves.
But wherever they are, and in every place where they live, the laws of the countries do not release them from the law of their Christ.
Nor does the fate assigned by the rulers compel them to use things that are unclean for them.
But sickness and health, wealth and poverty—things that are not within their freedom of choice—the place where they are imposes on them.
For just as human freedom is not governed by the compulsion of the seven planets, and when it is governed,
it can resist their governance, so too this visible human being cannot readily escape the command of his rulers.
For he is a servant and subject to authority. For if we could do everything, we ourselves would be everything; and if nothing were within our power to do, we would be the instruments
of others. But when God wills, all things can happen without hindrance.
For nothing can restrain that great and holy will. Even those who think they stand against it
stand not through strength, but through wickedness and error. And this can last only a short time,
because he is kind and allows all natures to remain what they are and to conduct themselves according to their own will.
Yet they are bound by the works that were made and by the arrangements established for their benefit.
For the order and governance that have been given, and the mingling of one with another, temper the fierceness of the natures, so that they do not cause complete harm,
nor suffer complete harm, as they used to cause and suffer harm before the creation of the world.
And a time is destined to come when even this harm that persists among them will end, through the instruction that takes place in another mingling.
And when that new world is established, all evil impulses will cease, all rebellions will end, the foolish will be persuaded, and all deficiencies will be made good.

And there will be peace and harmony through the gift of the Lord of all natures.
The Book of the Laws of the Countries is finished.
